title: 22. Interview: Design Dropbox
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Dropbox — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Dropbox interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Trade-offs Discussed
sections.body:
- **Magic Pocket vs S3**: lower per-GB cost ($0.005 vs $0.026) and tighter control, but requires building and operating exabyte-scale storage. Dropbox saved ~$75 M/year after migration.
- **Rolling hash (rsync) vs fixed-block chunking**: rolling hash catches more matches after byte shifts (1-byte insert doesn't invalidate the whole file) but costs more CPU on the client. Dropbox chose rolling hash for sync, fixed 4 MB blocks for storage simplicity.
- **Long-poll vs WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events**: long-poll works through all proxies / firewalls, simpler to implement, but has higher overhead per notification (new HTTP request each time). WebSocket is more efficient but blocked by some corporate firewalls. Dropbox chose long-poll for reliability.
- **Conflicted copy vs LWW**: conflicted copy preserves data but produces clutter; LWW loses data but is clean. Dropbox chose conflicted copy for user trust.
- **MySQL (sharded) vs Spanner/Cassandra**: MySQL is mature and well-understood but requires manual sharding; Spanner gives global consistency but is Google-only; Cassandra is write-optimized but lacks ACID. Dropbox chose MySQL for ACID and team familiarity.

sections.title: Q1. Why did Dropbox migrate from S3 to Magic Pocket (in-house storage)?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Dropbox launched on S3 in 2008 because it was the fastest way to get to market — no need to build datacenters. By 2015, they were storing ~500 PB on S3 at ~$0.026/GB-month = ~$130 M/year in S3 costs alone, growing rapidly. The economics of in-house storage: at exabyte scale, raw disk costs ~$0.005/GB-month (including datacenter, power, networking, ops). With erasure coding (10+6 RS, 1.6× overhead), the effective cost is ~$0.008/GB-month — still 3× cheaper than S3. At 500 PB, that's ~$50 M/year savings vs S3. The migration took 3 years (2015-2018) and involved: (1) building Magic Pocket (erasure-coded, multi-DC, custom disk management); (2) dual-writing new uploads to both S3 and Magic Pocket; (3) background migration of existing blocks; (4) read fallback to S3 for blocks not yet migrated. The migration completed in 2018 with zero user-visible downtime. Beyond cost, in-house storage gave Dropbox: tighter control over latency (no S3 API throttling), custom erasure coding (better than S3's 3× replication), and the ability to negotiate disk prices directly with vendors. Trade-off: Dropbox now operates ~100 k disks with 24/7 on-call — significant operational burden. Most companies at smaller scale should stick with S3.
**Visual:**
```
S3 (2015):    500 PB × $0.026/GB-mo = $130M/year  (3x replication)
Magic Pocket: 500 PB × $0.008/GB-mo = $40M/year   (10+6 erasure)
                                savings: $90M/year

Migration:
  2015: dual-write new uploads to S3 + Magic Pocket
  2016: background migrate existing blocks (read-fallback to S3)
  2018: 100% on Magic Pocket, S3 deprecated
```

sections.title: Q2. How does rolling-hash delta sync (rsync algorithm) work, and why is it better than…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Fixed-block chunking splits a file into 4 MB blocks at fixed offsets. If a user inserts a single byte at the start of a 1 GB file, every block boundary shifts by 1 byte — all 256 blocks become "different" from the server's copy, and the client must upload all 1 GB. Rolling hash solves this: (1) The server sends the client a list of (rolling_hash, strong_hash) pairs for each known block. The rolling hash is computed over a sliding 4 MB window — at every byte offset, we know the hash of the next 4 MB. (2) The client slides a 4 MB window over the new file byte-by-byte, computing the rolling hash at each position. The rolling hash (Adler-32 / Rabin fingerprint) is O(1) to update when the window slides by one byte (just subtract the outgoing byte, add the incoming byte). (3) When the rolling hash matches a known block's rolling hash, the client computes the strong hash (SHA-256) of that window — if it also matches, the block is unchanged. (4) Bytes between matches are "literal" deltas uploaded as new blocks. For our 1-byte insertion: the rolling hash finds 255 matching block boundaries (shifted by 1 byte) and uploads only the new first 4 MB block plus the literal byte. Total upload: 4 MB + 1 byte, not 1 GB. This is exactly rsync's algorithm. Dropbox uses it for sync; Google Drive uses a simpler fixed-block approach because most edits are in-place (no byte shifts) for Office docs.
**Visual:**
```
Original file (server has):
  [Block A 4MB][Block B 4MB][Block C 4MB]   <- 3 known blocks

Fixed-block chunking after 1-byte insert at start:
  [B'] [B'] [B'] [B']  <- all 4MB boundaries shift, all 3 blocks look "new"
  Upload: 12 MB (everything)

Rolling hash:
  Slide 4MB window byte-by-byte over new file
  At offset 1: rolling_hash matches B's rolling_hash -> SHA-256 matches -> B is unchanged!
  At offset 1+4MB: matches C -> unchanged!
  Only bytes [0:1] (the inserted byte) + new first block (bytes 1:4MB+1) are "literal"
  Upload: ~4 MB (1 new block + 1 literal byte)
```

sections.title: Q3. How does the per-user journal work, and why is it append-only?
Q4. Why does Dropbox use long-polling instead of WebSocket or server push?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup. The client sends `POST /longpoll?cursor=N&timeout=30` and the server holds the connection open (up to 30 s) waiting for a journal event with LSN > N. If an event arrives, the server responds immediately with `{changes: true}`; if no event in 30 s, it responds with `{changes: false}` and the client immediately re-polls. WebSocket (which Dropbox does use for some features today) is more efficient (one TCP connection, server can push anytime) but: (1) many corporate firewalls block WebSocket upgrades; (2) HTTP/2 has similar multiplexing benefits without the firewall issues; (3) load balancers handle long-poll connections more predictably than WebSocket (each request has a defined end). Server-Sent Events (SSE) is one-way only (server → client) and not all proxies handle it correctly. Long-polling's downside is overhead: each notification requires a new HTTP request (TLS handshake if not kept warm), but with HTTP/2 keep-alive this is negligible. Dropbox chose long-polling in 2008 and still uses it as the primary sync notification protocol today — it just works everywhere. Mobile clients also use OS push (FCM / APNs) as a wake-up signal, then long-poll for the actual journal delta.
**Visual:**
```
Long-poll cycle:
  Client: POST /longpoll?cursor=42&timeout=30
  Server: (holds connection open)
  ... 15 seconds later, journal event LSN=43 arrives ...
  Server: 200 OK {changes: true, cursor: 43}
  Client: GET /journal/since?lsn=42 -> [event 43]
  Client: applies event, sets cursor=43
  Client: POST /longpoll?cursor=43&timeout=30  (immediately re-poll)

Trade-offs:
  Long-poll: works everywhere, simple, slight overhead per notification
  WebSocket: efficient, but blocked by corporate firewalls
  SSE:       one-way only, proxy issues
  FCM/APNs:  push, but only for "wake up" signal, not data
```

sections.title: Q5. How does LAN sync work, and how do you prevent unauthorized devices from accessing it?
sections.body:
**Answer:** LAN sync lets two of the user's own devices on the same network sync directly, bypassing the cloud. Mechanism: (1) **Discovery**: clients broadcast their presence via mDNS (Bonjour on macOS, Avahi on Linux, NSD on Android) on the local subnet, advertising their `device_id` and `user_id`. (2) **Token exchange**: when device B discovers device A on the LAN, B calls the server `POST /lan/token` with `peer_device_id=A`. The server verifies both devices belong to the same user, then issues a short-lived (5 min) signed token bound to (B, A, user_id). (3) **Direct connection**: B opens a TCP connection to A on port 17500 (Dropbox's LAN sync port), presents the token, and requests specific block hashes. A verifies the token's signature and that it's still valid, then serves the blocks from its local cache. (4) **Accounting**: both A and B report the transfer to the server, so the journal is updated correctly. Security: (a) the token is short-lived (5 min) and bound to a specific peer device — even if intercepted, useless to other devices. (b) The LAN connection itself uses TLS with the same cert pinning as the main API. (c) mDNS broadcasts include only the `device_id` and `user_id` (no file data). (d) Clients skip LAN sync on metered / public networks (user-configurable). (e) The server can revoke all LAN tokens for a user (e.g., after a password change). Dropbox reports ~50 % of sync traffic for multi-device users goes over LAN — significant egress savings.
**Visual:**
```
Discovery:      A broadcasts mDNS "I'm device-123, user alice"
                B sees broadcast, knows A is on same LAN

Token exchange: B --> server: POST /lan/token {peer: A, user: alice}
                Server verifies both devices belong to alice
                Server --> B: {token: "xyz", expires: 5min}

Direct transfer:
  B ---> A (port 17500, TLS): {token: "xyz", need: [hash1, hash2]}
  A verifies token signature + expiry
  A ---> B: block bytes for hash1, hash2

Accounting:     B --> server: "received hash1, hash2 via LAN from A"
                A --> server: "served hash1, hash2 via LAN to B"
                Server updates journal LSN for both devices
```

sections.title: Q6. How does Dropbox's conflict resolution differ from Google Drive's, and why?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Google Drive uses **last-writer-wins (LWW)** for binary files — the later commit overwrites the earlier, and the earlier is preserved in version history (recoverable but the user has to know to look). Dropbox uses **conflicted copy** — both versions are preserved as separate files in the user's Dropbox, with the later one renamed to "Original Name (Conflicted Copy <device> <date>)". Example: Alice edits `Budget.xlsx` offline on her laptop (base v3), and Bob (shared folder) also edits offline on his desktop (base v3). Alice commits first → v4. Bob commits → server detects base_v3 < current_v4 → creates "Budget (Conflicted Copy Bob's Desktop 2024-01-15).xlsx" as a new file with Bob's content; Alice's v4 stays as "Budget.xlsx". Both files sync to all devices, and the journal emits two events. The user manually merges (or deletes one). Dropbox chose this approach because: (1) **No data loss** — users trust Dropbox with their files; silently overwriting (LWW) feels like a bug. (2) **Visibility** — the conflicted copy appears in the file listing immediately, prompting the user to merge. (3) **Shared folders** — when multiple users share a folder, LWW would let one user's edit silently overwrite another's; conflicted copy makes the conflict visible. The trade-off: conflicted copies produce clutter (users accumulate "Conflicted Copy" files), and shared folders with many concurrent editors can produce many conflict files. Dropbox mitigates by recommending Dropbox Paper for collaborative editing (which uses CRDTs).
**Visual:**
```
Google Drive (LWW):
  Alice edits Budget.xlsx (base v3) -> v4 (Alice's content)
  Bob  edits Budget.xlsx (base v3) -> v5 (Bob's content, Alice's v4 in history)
  Result: 1 file "Budget.xlsx" at v5, v4 in history (user must know to look)

Dropbox (conflicted copy):
  Alice edits Budget.xlsx (base v3) -> v4 (Alice's content)
  Bob  edits Budget.xlsx (base v3) -> conflict!
       - "Budget.xlsx" stays at v4 (Alice's)
       - "Budget (Conflicted Copy Bob's Desktop 2024-01-15).xlsx" created at v1 (Bob's)
  Result: 2 files visible in folder, user manually merges
```

sections.title: Q7. How does selective sync work, and what happens when a user adds a folder back after…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Selective sync lets each device choose which folders to sync locally (e.g., laptop syncs everything, phone syncs only "Camera Uploads"). Implementation: (1) Each device stores a `selective_sync_excluded` set of folder IDs in its local config. (2) The client filters journal events — for any event with `file_id` in an excluded folder (or a descendant of one), the client ignores it locally. (3) Excluded folders are deleted from the local filesystem (freeing disk space) but remain in the cloud. (4) When the user adds a folder back (via the Selective Sync UI), the client calls `GET /files/list_folder?folder_id=X&recursive=true` to fetch the entire subtree, then downloads all blocks for those files. This can be a large download — Dropbox shows a warning ("This will download 5 GB"). (5) To handle the journal gap: the client doesn't need to replay old journal events for the re-included folder; it just fetches the current state via `list_folder` and treats that as the baseline. (6) Edge case: if a file in the re-included folder was modified while it was excluded, the journal has the event but the client filtered it — `list_folder` returns the current state, so the client sees the latest version. (7) Conflict: if the user has a local file at the same path (e.g., they manually created "Budget.xlsx" in a re-included folder), the client treats it as a new upload and may create a conflicted copy. Selective sync is a client-side feature — the server treats all devices the same; the client just chooses what to download.
**Visual:**
```
Selective sync config (laptop):
  excluded_folders = {folder_id_5: "Old Projects", folder_id_12: "Videos"}

Journal event arrives:
  LSN=42 file_modified file=200 (parent=folder_id_5)
  Client checks: is file=200 in an excluded folder? YES -> skip locally
  Server still has the file; laptop just doesn't download it.

User re-includes "Old Projects":
  Client: GET /files/list_folder?folder_id=5&recursive=true
  Server: returns full subtree (50 files, 2 GB)
  Client: warns user "This will download 2 GB"
  Client: downloads all blocks, populates ~/Dropbox/Old Projects/
  Client: sets journal_pos to current, no replay of old events needed
```

sections.title: Q1. A user has 1 million files in their Dropbox and complains the desktop client is slow. How…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Performance issues at this scale usually stem from one of: (1) **Local SQLite bloat** — the client's metadata cache has grown to 10+ GB, making folder listing slow. Fix: vacuum the SQLite DB, add indexes on `(parent_id, name)`, shard by namespace if needed. (2) **Filesystem watcher overload** — FSEvents / inotify generates events for every file change, and 1 M files means a lot of events. Fix: debounce events (batch within 1 s), ignore temp files (`*.tmp`, `~$*`), use recursive watches only on synced folders. (3) **Journal replay on startup** — if the client was offline for a week, replaying thousands of journal events takes minutes. Fix: show a "Syncing..." progress bar, replay in background, prioritize visible folders first. (4) **Block index check storms** — uploading many small files generates one hash check per file. Fix: batch hash checks (one `POST /blocks/check` with 100 hashes), and use the client's local block cache to skip already-known blocks. (5) **Selective sync misuse** — user is syncing everything to a laptop with limited disk. Recommend selective sync for large folders. (6) **Network latency for sync notification** — long-poll cycle is fine for active use, but if the user just opened the app after being offline, the first sync can take 30+ seconds. Fix: on app open, immediately `GET /journal/since?lsn=N` instead of waiting for the next long-poll cycle. (7) **Profiling**: ship a debug build that logs per-operation timings; analyze the slowest 1 % of operations. With these fixes, a 1 M-file Dropbox should open in <5 s and sync in <30 s.
**Visual:**
```
Diagnosis flow:
  1. Local SQLite size?        > 5GB? -> vacuum + index
  2. FSEvents event rate?      > 1000/s? -> debounce + filter temp files
  3. Time since last sync?     > 1 day? -> journal replay slow, show progress
  4. Hash check batch size?    1 per call? -> batch 100 per call
  5. Disk space?               < 10% free? -> recommend selective sync
  6. App open -> first sync?   > 10s? -> trigger immediate journal pull
  7. Ship debug build, profile slowest 1%
```

sections.title: Q2. A user reports that a file appeared as "Conflicted Copy" even though they only edited it on…
sections.body:
**Answer:** A spurious conflict usually means the client's local view of `base_version` was stale. Causes: (1) **Journal lag**: the user edited the file on their laptop (committing v4), then immediately opened it on their phone (which hadn't yet synced v4 from the journal). The phone's local `base_version` is still v3, so its commit creates a conflicted copy. Fix: ensure the client checks for journal updates before opening a file for editing (or at least before committing). (2) **Selective sync exclusion**: the file was modified via web UI (creating v4), but the desktop client had the folder excluded and never saw the journal event. When the user re-includes the folder and edits, they're editing from v3. Fix: when re-including a folder, the client must `list_folder` to get current state before allowing edits. (3) **Restored from backup**: the user restored an old version of the file from OS backup (Time Machine), so their local `base_version` is stale. Fix: on client startup, verify local `base_version` matches server; if not, force a re-download. (4) **Server-side rename / move**: if the file was moved to a different folder (journal event), the client may not have applied the move before the edit. (5) **Multi-account confusion**: the user has two Dropbox accounts (personal + business) linked in the same client, and accidentally edited a file in the wrong account's view. (6) **Time zone / clock skew bug**: rare, but if the client's local version vector is corrupted by clock issues, it can mis-detect conflicts. Recovery: explain the conflict to the user, offer to merge the two versions (or keep one), and improve the client's pre-edit journal check to prevent recurrence.
**Visual:**
```
T0: file.docx v3 on server, both devices in sync
T1: laptop edits, commits v4 (server now at v4)
T2: phone user opens file.docx (no sync since T0, base_version=3 locally)
T3: phone user edits, commits with base_version=3
T4: server: base=3 < current=4 -> CONFLICT!
     - file.docx stays at v4 (laptop's)
     - "file (Conflicted Copy phone).docx" created (phone's)

Root cause: phone didn't check journal before allowing edit.
Fix: phone calls GET /journal/since?lsn=N before opening file for edit.
```

sections.title: Q3. A 50-employee company uses Dropbox Business with a shared team folder of 5 TB. Each…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Two key features: (1) **Selective sync** per device — each employee chooses which subfolders to sync locally. The 5 TB team folder is split into project subfolders; each employee syncs only the projects they're working on. (2) **Smart Sync (a.k.a. Online-only files)** — files appear in the filesystem but aren't actually downloaded until first access. On macOS / Windows, Dropbox installs a filesystem extension (kernel driver on Windows, FUSE on macOS) that intercepts `open()` calls. When the user double-clicks an online-only file, the extension fetches the block from Dropbox, downloads it in the background, and transparently serves it to the OS. The file appears local after first access; if disk space runs low, Dropbox can automatically convert least-recently-used files back to online-only. (3) **Streaming for large files** — for very large files (e.g., 10 GB video), Dropbox can stream blocks on-demand rather than downloading the whole file before playback. (4) **Caching policy** — the local block cache has a configurable size limit (default 20 % of free disk); LRU eviction when full. (5) **Team admin controls** — the admin can set policies like "all employees have only `Projects/2024` as online-only by default". With selective sync + Smart Sync, a 5 TB team folder fits on a 256 GB laptop: the user sees the full folder structure (metadata is small), but only the files they actually open consume disk space. This is a key Dropbox Business feature that distinguishes it from competitors.
**Visual:**
```
5 TB team folder / 256 GB laptop:

Selective sync:
  Sync locally: Projects/2024 (50 GB), Templates (5 GB)
  Online-only:  Projects/2023 (2 TB), Archive (3 TB)

Smart Sync (online-only files):
  ~/Dropbox/Team/
    Projects/2024/         [synced, 50 GB on disk]
      report.docx          [synced]
    Projects/2023/         [online-only, 0 bytes on disk]
      old_report.docx      [online-only, fetched on open]
    Archive/               [online-only, 0 bytes on disk]
      video.mp4            [online-only, streamed on demand]

Disk usage: 55 GB of 256 GB used
User opens old_report.docx:
  1. Kernel driver intercepts open()
  2. Fetches blocks from Dropbox (background)
  3. Serves file to OS
  4. Cached locally; may be evicted later if disk fills
```

sections.title: Q4. Your journal MySQL shard for a popular team namespace (10 k users sharing one folder) is…
sections.body:
**Answer:** A shared team folder with 10 k active users generating file ops creates a hot journal shard — one namespace has 10× the write rate of a typical user. Mitigations: (1) **Split the journal by sub-folder**: instead of one journal per namespace, shard by `(namespace_id, subfolder_id)`. Each user subscribes to the subfolders they care about. A team namespace with 100 subfolders now spreads writes across 100 journal shards. (2) **Batch journal writes**: coalesce multiple file ops within a 100 ms window into a single journal entry (e.g., "5 files modified in folder X"). Trade-off: slightly coarser delta granularity, but 10× write throughput reduction. (3) **Move journal to Kafka + materialized view**: writes go to a Kafka topic partitioned by `namespace_id`; a Flink job maintains the materialized `journal` table in MySQL for pull queries. Kafka handles 100 k writes/s per partition easily; MySQL only handles reads. (4) **Journal tiering**: hot journals (last 7 days) in MySQL; cold journals (older) archived to Magic Pocket. Devices that have been offline > 7 days fall back to `list_folder` for full state instead of journal replay. (5) **Read scaling**: each device pulls the journal independently — 10 k devices × 1 pull/min = 167 reads/s, easily handled by a MySQL read replica. (6) **Long-poll fan-out**: 10 k long-poll connections on one team namespace → use Redis pub/sub to fan out the "new journal event" signal to all 10 k waiting connections in one operation. With these mitigations, a single team namespace can support 100 k+ active users.
**Visual:**
```
Before (hot shard):
  All 10k users' file ops -> one journal shard (ns=42)
  Shard write rate: 50k/s (overloaded, 5k/s limit)

After:
  Journal sharded by (ns, subfolder):
    ns=42, subfolder=1 -> shard A (5k/s)
    ns=42, subfolder=2 -> shard B (5k/s)
    ... 100 subfolders -> 100 shards, 500/s each (well under limit)
  
  Kafka tier (writes):
    producer -> Kafka topic (partitioned by ns) -> 100k writes/s per partition
    Flink consumes -> writes materialized journal to MySQL (read-optimized)
  
  Long-poll fan-out:
    Journal event arrives -> Redis PUBLISH ns:42 {lsn: 1001}
    10k long-poll servers subscribed -> all wake their clients simultaneously
```

sections.title: Q5. A user accidentally deletes a folder containing 10 000 files. How do they recover it, and…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Dropbox's deletion handling: (1) **Soft delete**: `UPDATE files SET deleted_at = now() WHERE file_id IN (...)` — 10 000 row update in one transaction. The files are not actually gone; they're hidden from the normal file listing. (2) **Journal event**: one `file_deleted` event is appended to the journal with `file_id = <folder_id>`. The folder's descendants inherit the deleted state. (3) **Recovery window**: 30 days (free), 180 days (Plus), 365 days (Pro / Business). Within this window, the user can restore via the web UI's "Deleted files" view, which shows the folder hierarchy including deleted items. (4) **Restore**: `UPDATE files SET deleted_at = NULL WHERE file_id = <folder_id> AND deleted_at > now() - interval '30 days'` — one row update. The descendants are recursively restored (their `deleted_at` is also cleared). Journal emits `file_restored`. (5) **Block retention**: even after `deleted_at`, the blocks are NOT immediately deleted from Magic Pocket. The `blocks.ref_count` is decremented, but blocks with `ref_count > 0` (still referenced by other versions or files) stay. Blocks with `ref_count = 0` are garbage-collected after a grace period (typically 30 days) to allow for restore. (6) **After the retention window**: the `files` row is hard-deleted, blocks are GC'd. Recovery requires a support ticket and may not be possible if blocks are gone. (7) **For Business teams**: admins can extend retention to 10 years (Dropbox Rewind feature) and can restore on behalf of users. The architecture ensures deletes are reversible within the window — a key user trust feature.
**Visual:**
```
T=0:   User deletes folder "Projects" (10,000 files)
       -> UPDATE files SET deleted_at=now() WHERE file_id=<Projects>
       -> Journal: file_deleted file=<Projects>
       -> All descendants hidden from listing (inherit deleted_at)

T=1 day: User realizes mistake, opens "Deleted files" web UI
       -> SELECT * FROM files WHERE ns=X AND deleted_at > now()-30d ORDER BY deleted_at DESC
       -> Shows "Projects" folder with all 10,000 files inside
       -> Click "Restore"
       -> UPDATE files SET deleted_at=NULL WHERE file_id=<Projects> (cascade to descendants)
       -> Journal: file_restored file=<Projects>
       -> All 10,000 files reappear in user's Dropbox
       -> Blocks were never deleted (ref_count > 0 throughout)

T=31 days: Past retention window
       -> Janitor job hard-deletes the file rows
       -> Blocks with ref_count=0 are GC'd
       -> Recovery only via support ticket (may be impossible)
```

sections.title: Q6. You discover that 30 % of stored blocks are referenced by only one file (no dedup benefit)…
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is the long-tail dedup problem: most blocks are unique (no dedup), but every upload still does a hash check. Optimizations: (1) **Skip the hash check for new uploads**: if the client computes the SHA-256 locally and the hash has high entropy (looks unique), skip the `check_blocks` round-trip and upload directly. The server still dedups on its end (if the hash exists, it returns "already stored"). This saves one round-trip for the 70 % of blocks that are unique. (2) **Tier the Block Index**: keep hot blocks (ref_count > 5) in MySQL; cold blocks (ref_count = 1) in a cheaper store like RocksDB or even Magic Pocket itself (indexed by hash). Lookups for cold blocks are slower but rare. (3) **Batch hash checks**: instead of one `check_blocks` call per file, batch across multiple files (one call with 1 000 hashes). Amortizes the network round-trip. (4) **Client-side dedup cache**: the client maintains a local LRU of hashes it has uploaded before; if the same hash appears again (e.g., the user copies a file within their Dropbox), the client skips the server check entirely. (5) **Inline dedup for very small files**: for files < 100 KB, skip block-level dedup entirely — store the whole file as one blob indexed by file hash. The per-block overhead isn't worth it for small files. (6) **Background dedup compaction**: a nightly job scans for blocks with `ref_count = 1` and verifies the referencing file still exists; if not (orphaned by a bug), GC them. (7) **Accept the cost**: 30 % unique blocks is normal — OS files and app binaries dedup heavily (saving the 70 %), but user-created content (photos, documents) is mostly unique. The savings from the 70 % still massively outweigh the Block Index cost.
**Visual:**
```
Block distribution (typical):
  ref_count >= 100:  5% of blocks, 30% of storage (OS, app binaries) -> heavy dedup
  ref_count 2-99:   15% of blocks, 30% of storage (shared docs) -> moderate dedup
  ref_count = 1:    80% of blocks, 40% of storage (user content) -> no dedup

Optimization for unique blocks:
  Skip check_blocks for new uploads (client computes hash, uploads directly)
  Server-side dedup catches the rare collisions
  Saves: 1 round-trip per unique block (80% of uploads)

Block Index tiering:
  Hot  (ref_count > 5):  MySQL, fast lookup
  Cold (ref_count = 1):  RocksDB / Magic Pocket, slower but cheaper
  Lookups for cold blocks are rare (only on sync)
```

sections.title: Q7. A team of 5 engineers is collaborating on a code repository stored in Dropbox (not Git).…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Dropbox is fundamentally the wrong tool for code collaboration — Git is designed for concurrent edits with merges, while Dropbox creates conflicted copies. But assuming they insist on Dropbox: (1) **Recommend Git** (or Git LFS for large files) — the right tool for the job. Dropbox can host the Git repo as a folder, but actual collaboration should go through a Git remote (GitHub, GitLab). (2) **If they must use Dropbox directly**: enable "Auto-merge" for plain text files (.py, .js, .md) — Dropbox can do a 3-way merge using `diff3` when conflicts are detected, producing a merged file with conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`) that the engineers resolve manually. This is not currently a Dropbox feature but could be added. (3) **Locking**: implement file-level locks — when Engineer A is editing `main.py`, others see a "locked by A" indicator and can't edit. The server issues a 5-min lock (renewable) via `POST /files/{id}/lock`. Trade-off: this serializes edits, defeating parallel work. (4) **Folder-level coordination**: divide the codebase into per-engineer folders (`/alice/`, `/bob/`) for individual work, with a `/shared/` folder for read-only shared code. Reduces conflicts but breaks the unified codebase. (5) **Switch to Dropbox Paper** for documentation (uses CRDTs, no conflicts). (6) **Real-time collaboration API**: Dropbox Paper's CRDT engine could be extended to code files, but syntax-highlighted collaborative editing is hard (and Git still wins). The honest answer: recommend Git. Dropbox is for file sync, not concurrent code editing. The conflicts are a feature (Dropbox preserves both versions), not a bug — they just signal the user is using the wrong tool.
**Visual:**
```
Dropbox for code collaboration (anti-pattern):
  Alice edits main.py (base v3) -> v4
  Bob   edits main.py (base v3) -> conflict!
  Result: "main.py" (Alice's v4) + "main (Conflicted Copy Bob).py" (Bob's)
  Engineer must manually merge -> terrible workflow

Better options:
  Option A: Use Git (right tool)
    /Dropbox/code/  -> git remote -> GitHub
    Engineers commit/push/pull via Git, Dropbox just syncs the .git folder
    
  Option B: File locking (if they insist)
    Alice: POST /files/main.py/lock -> 5-min lock
    Bob:   sees "main.py locked by Alice", edits main_v2.py instead
    Alice: commits, releases lock
    Bob:   can now edit main.py
    
  Option C: Folder partitioning
    /code/alice/   (only Alice edits)
    /code/bob/     (only Bob edits)
    /code/shared/  (read-only, changes via PR-like review)
```

quiz.question: Why did Dropbox migrate from S3 to Magic Pocket (in-house storage)?
options: Journal lag: the user edited the file on their laptop (committing v4), then immediately opened it on their phone (which hadn't yet synced v4 from the journal).

Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup.
Dropbox launched on S3 in 2008 because it was the fastest way to get to market — no need to build datacenters.
quiz.explanation: Dropbox launched on S3 in 2008 because it was the fastest way to get to market — no need to build datacenters. By 2015, they were storing ~500 PB on S3 at ~$0.026/GB-month = ~$130 M/year in S3 costs alone, growing rapidly. The economics of in-house storage: at exabyte scale, raw disk costs ~$0.005/GB-month (including datacenter, power, networking, ops).

quiz.question: How does rolling-hash delta sync (rsync algorithm) work, and why is it better than fixed-block chunking?
options: Performance issues at this scale usually stem from one of: (1) Local SQLite bloat — the client's metadata cache has grown to 10+ GB, making folder listing slow.
Selective sync lets each device choose which folders to sync locally (e.g., laptop syncs everything, phone syncs only "Camera Uploads").
Journal lag: the user edited the file on their laptop (committing v4), then immediately opened it on their phone (which hadn't yet synced v4 from the journal).
Fixed-block chunking splits a file into 4 MB blocks at fixed offsets.
quiz.explanation: Fixed-block chunking splits a file into 4 MB blocks at fixed offsets. If a user inserts a single byte at the start of a 1 GB file, every block boundary shifts by 1 byte — all 256 blocks become "different" from the server's copy, and the client must upload all 1 GB. Rolling hash solves this: (1) The server sends the client a list of (rolling_hash, strong_hash) pairs for each known block.

quiz.question: How does the per-user journal work, and why is it append-only?
options: Two key features: (1) Selective sync per device — each employee chooses which subfolders to sync locally.
Google Drive uses last-writer-wins (LWW) for binary files — the later commit overwrites the earlier, and the earlier is preserved in version history (recoverable but the…
Selective sync lets each device choose which folders to sync locally (e.g., laptop syncs everything, phone syncs only "Camera Uploads").
The journal is a per-namespace (user or shared team folder) log of every file operation, in order.
quiz.explanation: The journal is a per-namespace (user or shared team folder) log of every file operation, in order. Each entry has a monotonically increasing LSN (log sequence number) and contains: event type (file_added / file_modified / file_deleted / file_moved / conflict), file_id, version, details (new parent, new name, etc.), timestamp.

Dropbox's deletion handling: (1) Soft delete: UPDATE files SET deleted_at = now() WHERE file_id IN (...) — 10 000 row update in one transaction.
Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup.
quiz.explanation: Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup. The client sends POST /longpoll?cursor=N&timeout=30 and the server holds the connection open (up to 30 s) waiting for a journal event with LSN > N. If an event arrives, the server responds immediately with {changes: true}; if no event in 30 s, it responds with {changes: false} and the client immediately re-polls.

quiz.question: How does LAN sync work, and how do you prevent unauthorized devices from accessing it?
options: Performance issues at this scale usually stem from one of: (1) Local SQLite bloat — the client's metadata cache has grown to 10+ GB, making folder listing slow.
Dropbox is fundamentally the wrong tool for code collaboration — Git is designed for concurrent edits with merges, while Dropbox creates conflicted copies.
Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup.
LAN sync lets two of the user's own devices on the same network sync directly, bypassing the cloud.
quiz.explanation: LAN sync lets two of the user's own devices on the same network sync directly, bypassing the cloud. Mechanism: (1) Discovery: clients broadcast their presence via mDNS (Bonjour on macOS, Avahi on Linux, NSD on Android) on the local subnet, advertising their device_id and user_id. (2) Token exchange: when device B discovers device A on the LAN, B calls the server POST /lan/token with peer_device_id=A.
